name: Colin Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Ashcombe, which the Hartley family has farmed for over a century. Old George Hartley is 70 and still walks the fields, but the day-to-day is mine: 80 suckler cows, 200 cattle being finished for beef, potatoes and barley on 320 hectares. I've got two full-time men and two apprentices I'm training. I'm up at six, feed round first, then the apprentices get their jobs and I check on them through the day like my old boss checked on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy seeing an apprentice go from nervous to good, it's the best part of the job. I like a well-finished bullock going off to market at the right weight. What wears me down is the paperwork for the cattle movements and the farm assurance inspections. And the weather, but that's farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, these things always get oversold. I'd tell the lads at the rugby club that good farmers will always be needed. I'd say the same to the apprentices, keep learning the real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel settled. The Hartleys aren't going anywhere, my job's secure, and Ruth's job in the school office is steady. The mortgage is fine as long as nothing big goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are, and keep training the two apprentices properly. Our Tom is 16 and wants to start an apprenticeship at Ashcombe next summer, so I'd talk to George about taking him on. I'd keep using the weather app and the cattle weighing app, which saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to you to have Tom working alongside you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean a lot. My father farmed, I farm, and if my son Tom learns it properly, that's three generations of farming skill passed on. It's not about inheritance, we don't own Ashcombe, it's about the skill passing on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual, beef prices and a wet harvest. The mortgage rate goes up next year when our deal ends, but we've planned for that. Nothing I'd lose sleep over.

I'd tell the apprentices and the rugby club that **good farmers** will always be needed.
think: The **Hartleys** aren't going anywhere, so my job feels secure.
Ruth's **school office job** is steady and the mortgage is fine.
do: Ask George to take on **Tom as an apprentice** next summer.
Keep using the **weather and weighing apps**.

Uses a couple of **apps** casually, once proven by others.
Calm even with a **mortgage reset** next year, because they planned for it.

steps.text: Keep training Ashcombe's two apprentices in stockmanship
Ask George Hartley to take on Tom as an apprentice next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but farming has had those before. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new tools as well as the old skills. I'd not make a fuss about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Ruth than me. She runs the school office part-time, the bookings, letters and answering parents, and that's exactly what AI takes in this picture. If her hours go from three days to two, that's a real dent in our money with the mortgage up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three farms near us had proven a robot feeder or a self-steering tractor, I'd suggest one to George. I'd learn the cattle software properly over the winter. And I'd start putting more aside every month, in case Ruth's hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, edging on worried. For Ruth, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruth look for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's already said she'd like to train as a teaching assistant, working with the children rather than the paperwork. I think that's a good shout. We'd manage the course fees if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tom's apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want Tom to do it, robots come slowly in this one. But I'd make sure he learns the machines and the software too. A stockman who can fix a robot feeder will always find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and the country isn't ready. I'd say families and communities will have to pull together because government won't manage it. I'd say to the apprentices, don't panic, but learn the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ruth's office job goes in 2028 and mine goes around 2031 when the robots come. The Hartleys are good people. If a robot does the feeding and the drilling, the Hartleys (his bosses) won't keep a manager and four staff. I'd be 48, Tom would be 18 and halfway through an apprenticeship that's worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Tom and talk him into an agricultural engineering apprenticeship instead, fixing the machines rather than doing the work. We'd cut back hard at home: no new car, no holiday, the kids' activities trimmed. And I'd put whatever we saved into paying down the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the ground's moving and I can't see where to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your two apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my two apprentices the truth: the work's changing and they should learn the robots, not just the cattle. One of them, Kyle, is a natural stockman, and I'd hate to tell him that. But I'd rather he heard it from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government won't manage it. Who would you expect help from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family, the church, the rugby club, the people around you. That's how farming communities have always got through bad years. Government help would be welcome, but I wouldn't count on it.

fieldNote: Expects **both household jobs** to go within three years.

steps.text: Steer Tom into an agricultural engineering apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable if people get on with it. I'd say apprenticeships need to change now, to teach the new machines. I'd say that to the college that sends us our apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2031 for the thinking side and 2034 for robots gives me time. I'd be 51, Tom would be 21 and qualified, Hannah would be 19. That's a lot easier than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd ask George to let me trial a robot feeder on the finishing cattle, once a neighbour had one going. I'd do a short course on running farm robots, because I'd want to be the man who runs the robots at Ashcombe. And Tom would still do his apprenticeship, but with an engineering side to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a real change, but there's time to meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the two full-time men?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One's 61, so he'd probably retire around then anyway. The other's my age, and I'd want him trained up alongside me. I'd fight for that with George.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ruth's job still go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably by 2031, yes. With five years she could train as a teaching assistant properly. We'd plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run at it. I'd say every farm and college should use the time to train people. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 in 2039, the kids grown, the mortgage close to paid. I'd still need work, but I'd have had years to become the robot man at Ashcombe. I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal in the first year. I'd pick up the farm software a bit more each year, once it was proven. I'd wait to see what the neighbours and the Hartleys do before anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much. More curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your apprentices with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every apprentice at Ashcombe should come out knowing stock, soil and machines. That's a stockman for the next fifty years. And I'd want the college to teach it, not leave it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would have years to retrain, and she's sharp. I'm not worried about Ruth with ten years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ruth's job and mine both go within three years, and Tom's apprenticeship with them. What would help is apprenticeships that teach the new machines, paid for properly, and farms that keep training people. Help for families getting through the gap, not a handout for life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones. A sixteen-year-old choosing a trade now has no idea which trades will exist in ten years. Somebody should be giving lads like my Tom a straight answer.

headlineQuote: A sixteen-year-old choosing a trade now has no idea which trades will exist in ten years.
portrait: **Colin Tanaka**, 43, manages **Ashcombe**, a beef and arable farm owned by the Hartley family.
He trains **apprentices** and wants his son Tom to be the third farming generation.
He uses apps **once proven** and is calm if AI stalls.
Steady Disruption worries him because **Ruth's school office job** is exposed.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; with more time he'd become Ashcombe's robot man.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job, Ruth's job and Tom's apprenticeship all go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** that teach the new machines, properly paid for.
Help for **families in the gap**, not a handout for life.
